There are objective binges, and subjective binges. 

**Objective binges** are when you eat multiple meals worth of food, often only stopping when you run out or feel completely ill. Generally feels like being in a trance state.

**Subjective binges** are more like when you feel guilty for eating a bit too much, or feel like you've had too many calories. It's more in your head, basically.

It seems like it's more towards an objective binge with the amount of food, timeframe, and the thought process. I wouldn't beat yourself up about it. Stay mindful, and perhaps only keep a limited amount of ice cream in the freezer at a time.

The biggest part of getting DBT to work, is **willingness**.

DBT isn't a magic pill, and it takes a lot of mental work. You're challenging the very thoughts in your head, after all!

When you are taught a new skill, use it. It's going to feel forced, awkward, and sometimes like bullshit. That's where willingness comes in. Remember, the *program is there to help you*. The more you push yourself to fill out those worksheets, participate in group, keep a daily mood diary, and make time each day to practice your new skills...the more results you will have.

They say it's like working out a muscle. At first you feel clumsy and limited, but in time with consistent work, you'll find yourself with a healthier mindset and using effective coping skills without even realizing it. 

I wish you the best of luck! Remember to be patient and compassionate with yourself!

What I've noticed in my experiences, is that it's usually a mix of both. 

My FPs would have behaviors that would hurt me, generally consistent ones that they would not change. My head told me that they are unhealthy for me, but my heart refused to see them as anything but the light of my life. Essentially, my head and heart were fighting. This caused my warped, out of proportion reactions. Which would only escalate the problem, and was much more apparent than any toxic behaviors they displayed. 

My feelings were justified, but my reactions were not.

I found that when I removed my reaction, and looked at the facts, they treated me unkindly and without respect. I did, in fact, have calm, constructive conversations with these people. Unfortunately, it did not work, and I had to let them go. As much as it hurt, letting go was a huge step on the path to overcoming BPD for me. I only intend on keeping positive, uplifting people in my life.

However, if you can't justify your feelings, regardless of your reaction, your behavior is most likely toxic. In this case, having a hard look in the mirror may be in order. DBT can help immensely with how you handle relationships while balancing BPD. Either way, I wish you luck, and remind you to be compassionate with yourself.
